newsitem.title: UK: Regional trade as vital to SAfrica as EU - official.
newsitem.headline: Regional trade as vital to SAfrica as EU - official.

text.p: Regional trade with other countries in southern Africa is as important to South Africa as its trade deal with the European Union (EU), Rob Davies, chairman of the South African parliament's Trade and Industry Committee, said.
He warned that the EU must match its professed political support for the new democratic South Africa with a fair trade arrangement for the country and region.

"The challenge is very much in Europe's court. Is Europe serious about seeing an arrangement which is going to promote development or is it simply going to seek a normal hard-nosed trade deal with us?" Davies added in an interview in London late Friday.
"At the moment our view is that the principles of solidarity appear to be conspicuous by their absense in current proposals."

South Africa has been refused membership of the Lome Convention which offers poorer countries trade concessions with Europe. It will start preliminary discussions on a trade deal with the EU, its largest trading partner, later this month.
Deputy president Thabo Mbeki, seen widely as successor to President Nelson Mandela, is on an eight-nation tour of the EU to garner support for South Africa's position.

Davies, who was travelling independently of Mbeki, said the current deal from the EU was not equitable and would undermine the smaller economies of other southern African countries linked to South Africa through a customs union.

"South Africa's economy is half that of Belgium's; our unemployment rate is 30 percent and we have a highly protected industrial sector undergoing a complicated transition partly driven by internally-imposed tariff reductions," he noted.

"We would get 4-7 percent additional duty-free access to the EU under all the obligations the EU would implement, but we would have to allow 36 percent duty-free access by the EU...a large adjustment for a rather small additional benefit."
Davies said that South Africa would demand in coming talks that its neighbours get priority access to its markets and a chance to consolidate their presence there before the EU was admitted.
Asked if that meant linking access for the EU to South Africa to regional countries' access, he replied: "That is something which is very significant and has to be taken on board."
Asked whether he felt South Africa had good trade relations with nearby countries, Davies acknowledged there was "very skewed and imbalanced trade" in the region.

But he said South Africa had signed a trade protocol under the auspices of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) in August which envisages negotiations leading to a free trade area within eight years.

There was also progress on a new revenue-sharing formula with South African Customs Union members, Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland, all of which would immediately feel the effect of a deal with the EU.

Davies said Europe was particularly sensitive about agricultural products. "They want to exclude about 40 percent of our current agricultural imports into the EU from a free trade area. But they want South Africa to allow in 95 percent of EU agricultural products duty-free and subsidised."
Such a deal would have a "devastating" effect on Namibia's beef industry and the Swazi sugar sector, among others.
